accepted.question_text: Given a block graph G, meaning a graph in which every block is a complete graph, and letting A(G) be its (0,1)-adjacency matrix, characterize exactly when G is nonsingular, that is, when A(G) is invertible (equivalently, G has full rank and nullity 0), as opposed to singular.

evidence.quote: An interesting open problem, proposed in 2013 by Bapat and Roy, is to characterize nonsingular block graphs.

Combinatorial formulae for the determinant of block graphs are known in terms of size and arrangements of its blocks [3, 16, 15]. But due to a myriad of possibilities of sizes and arrangements of the blocks in general, it is difficult to classify nonsingular or singular block graphs. Hence, it is an open problem [3].

accepted.question_text: If G is a connected block graph in which every block has order at least 3, must the nullity of G be at most 1? Here nullity means the number of zero eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix A(G).
accepted.context_brief: Nullity bound for K2-forbidden block graphs

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.6. Let G be a connected block graph where each block is of order at least 3. Then the nullity of G is at most 1.

accepted.question_text: Let G1 and G2 be two connected nonsingular block graphs, and let v1 be a vertex of G1 and v2 be a vertex of G2. If one adds a new edge between v1 and v2 and the resulting graph is still a block graph, must the resulting block graph also be nonsingular?
accepted.context_brief: Edge-joining conjecture for nonsingular block graphs

evidence.quote: Conjecture 4.2. Let G1 and G2 be two connected nonsingular block graphs. If we add an edge between vertices v1 and v2, v1 ∈ V (G1), v2 ∈ V (G2), then the resulting block graph is also nonsingular.
